strengths: Proposes a well-motivated generalization of prior solver-distillation parameterizations (LD3, S4S) by adding theoretically-guided additive corrections and a weighted sum of all previous points, which is shown both conceptually (Table 1) and empirically (Figure 3, Table 3) to stabilize and accelerate training compared to S4S under matched parameter budgets.

Adds adversarial training via a relativistic GAN loss (based on R3GAN) on top of the distillation loss, and provides a reasonably convincing qualitative/quantitative argument (Table 4, Figure 4) that this reduces artifacts in low-NFE regimes even when it slightly increases the raw distillation loss.

Broad and systematic experimental evaluation spanning pixel-space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2) and latent-space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256, Stable Diffusion on MS-COCO) settings, with consistent improvements over training-free solvers (UniPC, iPNDM) and training-based baselines (GITS, DMN, LD3, S4S) especially at low NFE.

Thorough ablations and efficiency analysis: dataset-size sensitivity (Appendix C.1), training-time and memory comparisons against LD3/S4S/CD/PD (Appendix C.2-C.3), GAN-weight robustness (Appendix B.3), inference-time overhead (negligible, Table 10), and cross-dataset generalization (Table 5).

Good reproducibility effort: detailed algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 1), full hyperparameter listings per dataset (Appendix D), and extensive qualitative sample galleries (random and selected) across all datasets and NFEs, including explicit discussion of mode-collapse absence.
weaknesses: The core novelty is largely a recombination/refinement of existing ideas (LD3/S4S-style solver distillation parameterizations plus a known GAN loss/backbone, R3GAN, and adversarial diffusion distillation techniques already used elsewhere), making the conceptual contribution somewhat incremental relative to the empirical thoroughness.

Performance gains are not uniform: at higher NFEs (e.g., MS-COCO NFE=6,7; CIFAR10 NFE=8) GAS is sometimes narrowly outperformed by S4S variants, and the paper itself notes FID becomes unreliable beyond NFE≈8, yet such comparisons are still reported without a more robust perceptual/human evaluation to corroborate claims.

The method introduces meaningful additional complexity (separate parameter sets θ, φ, ξ, choice of base solver for theoretical guidance, discriminator architecture/training schedule) and, as acknowledged by the authors, requires separate training per target NFE and relies on full backpropagation through the ODE solve, raising scalability concerns for larger models/resolutions that are not empirically tested (largest resolution shown is 512×512 with only 1k-2k training iterations and a small 128-sample validation set).

No human perceptual study or CLIP-score/text-alignment metric is reported for the text-to-image (Stable Diffusion) experiments, despite these being the most practically relevant and highest-resolution setting; conclusions there rest solely on FID over 30k generations and a handful of qualitative examples.

Adversarial training roughly doubles-to-quadruples training time and adds a discriminator with its own hyperparameters/architecture dependence (pretrained R3GAN checkpoints for pixel-space vs. random-init for latent-space), which somewhat complicates the reproducibility and fairness of comparison against lighter-weight baselines like LD3/S4S that do not require this extra machinery.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated generalization of prior solver-distillation parameterizations (LD3, S4S): it uses a 'theoretical guidance' base solver (DPM-Solver++(3M)) with additive trainable corrections, removes the fixed-order restriction by allowing a weighted sum over all previous points/velocities, and initializes corrections at zero for stable training — a sensible and clearly explained design (Table 1, Eq. 12-20).

Combining distillation loss with adversarial training (relativistic R3GAN loss) is a reasonable idea to address blurriness/artifacts that plain regression-based solver distillation produces at low NFE, and the paper provides qualitative (Fig. 4, extensive appendix figures) and quantitative (Table 4) evidence that it helps detail fidelity.

Broad empirical coverage across 6 datasets spanning pixel-space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2) and latent-space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256) models as well as text-to-image Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO, with consistent comparisons against many baselines (DPM++, UniPC, iPNDM with GITS/DMN schedules, LD3, S4S).

Reasonably thorough ablations/analyses: isolated comparison of the GS parameterization against S4S under matched parameter counts (Table 3, Fig. 3) showing more stable/faster convergence; training-set-size sensitivity (Appendix C.1); GAN-loss-weight insensitivity (Appendix B.3/Fig. 6); cross-dataset transfer (Table 5); training time, memory, and inference-time overhead reporting (Tables 7-10).
Good reproducibility effort: explicit algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and detailed hyperparameter/training configuration appendix (Appendix D) for all datasets.
weaknesses: The claim of 'superior performance... across all evaluated datasets' is contradicted by the paper's own results: on MS-COCO (Table 2c), GAS underperforms S4S and LD3 at NFE=6 and NFE=7 (e.g., 11.73 vs. 10.83 for Best LD3, 11.91 vs. 11.17 for S4S at NFE=6), which is glossed over in the text.

The central ablation needed to justify the paper's framing is missing: since adversarial training appears to be the dominant driver of quality improvement at low NFE (Table 4, Fig. 4), the paper never tests adding the same R3GAN adversarial loss on top of the LD3/S4S baselines to isolate whether gains stem from the new Generalized Solver parameterization or simply from adding a GAN loss to any solver-distillation scheme. Without this, the attribution of improvement to the proposed parameterization is not well supported.

Evaluation relies essentially exclusively on FID (plus LPIPS/L1 as training losses), a metric the authors themselves note 'loses correlation with perceived fidelity at high NFEs' (Appendix D.2); no human evaluation, CLIP-score (for text-to-image), or other perceptual/diversity metrics are reported to substantiate claims about 'detail fidelity' and artifact removal, which instead rely on cherry-picked ('selected') qualitative examples.

Student models sometimes achieve FID scores better than the teacher's own FID (e.g., AFHQv2 teacher FID 2.60/2.16 vs. some student configurations), which is a known symptom of adversarial-loss-driven FID optimization/metric gaming rather than genuine improvement in matching the teacher's distribution; this is not sufficiently discussed or guarded against beyond a brief mode-collapse check.

The technical novelty is incremental relative to LD3/S4S (an additive-correction reparameterization plus removing the order restriction) and relative to standard use of adversarial losses in distillation (already used in diffusion distillation works such as Sauer et al. 2023/2024, Kim et al. 2023); the paper's distinct contribution is a fairly straightforward combination of known ingredients.

Practical costs are non-trivial (training time increases 2-4x, memory overhead, and the method still requires per-NFE-setting training as acknowledged in Limitations), yet the efficiency comparisons are made primarily against non-adversarial baselines (LD3, S4S), which somewhat understates the added resource cost relative to a fairer matched-resource comparison.

Some experimental choices (e.g., only 1000 training samples for Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO solver training, use of a 'student NFE+1' teacher rather than a high-quality fixed teacher) may limit the generality and robustness of the reported gains, and are not critically examined for their effect on the comparisons.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: instability and limited parameter space of existing solver-distillation methods (LD3, S4S), and the lack of fine-detail preservation in few-step ODE samplers.

The proposed Generalized Solver (GS) parameterization is a clean generalization that unifies/extends LD3 and S4S by adding theoretical (additive) guidance from a pre-defined high-order solver (DPM-Solver++(3M)) and a weighted sum of all previous points, which is shown both theoretically (Table 1) and empirically (Figure 3, Table 3) to improve training stability and convergence speed.

Combining distillation loss with an adversarial (relativistic GAN, R3GAN-based) loss is shown to meaningfully reduce artifacts and improve FID especially in low-NFE regimes, with clear qualitative support (Figure 4) and quantitative ablation (Table 4) showing that lower regression loss does not always correlate with better FID.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 6 datasets spanning pixel-space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2) and latent-space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256, MS-COCO with Stable Diffusion), with comparisons to multiple training-free solvers (UniPC, iPNDM, DPM++) and training-based competitors (GITS, DMN, LD3, S4S).

Thorough ablation studies: controlled comparison with S4S under equal parameter budgets, dataset-size efficiency analysis, training time/GPU memory/inference time overhead quantification, GAN-loss weight sensitivity analysis, and cross-dataset generalization tests (Table 5).

Strong reproducibility: detailed appendix with full hyperparameters, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), teacher generation protocol, and dataset/model configuration for every experiment, plus a code release statement.
Explicitly investigates and rules out mode collapse, a common risk when adding adversarial losses, via diverse random samples.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contribution largely combines/extends existing ideas (LD3/S4S-style trainable solver parameterization, DPM-Solver++ as theoretical backbone, and adversarial losses already used in diffusion distillation/GAN literature such as R3GAN) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

Gains over strong training-based baselines (e.g., S4S-Alt) shrink substantially at higher NFEs (e.g., CIFAR10 NFE=8/10, where GAS/GS results are nearly identical to S4S-Alt), and the paper itself notes FID loses correlation with perceptual quality above NFE≈8, undermining claims of consistent superiority across the full NFE range.

Evaluation relies heavily on FID and author-selected ("selected" vs "random") qualitative comparisons; no human/perceptual study is conducted to substantiate claims about improved "detail fidelity," leaving the central qualitative claim only weakly supported beyond cherry-picked figures.

GAS incurs non-trivial additional training cost and memory overhead relative to GS and other baselines (2-9 hours vs 1-2.5 hours, several GB extra memory), and as acknowledged, requires separate training per target NFE and may not scale well to larger images/models due to full backpropagation through the ODE solver — a notable limitation for the resource-constrained scenario the paper motivates itself with.

Several baseline numbers are taken directly from prior papers under potentially different teacher/training protocols (flagged with † in Table 2), which slightly weakens the fairness/consistency of some comparisons.

The notation and parameterization in Section 3.1 (especially Eqs. 15-20) is dense and could be better motivated/explained for readability; the mapping from the general signature to the final practical coefficients requires effort to follow.

strengths: Introduces a clean, well-motivated 'Generalized Solver' parameterization that unifies and generalizes prior solver-distillation methods (LD3, S4S) by adding theoretical guidance from a base multistep solver (DPM-Solver++) as an additive correction, and by including a weighted sum of previous points in the multistep signature; this is shown both conceptually and empirically to improve training stability/convergence (Table 3, Figure 3, Appendix B.1, B.9).

Combines the distillation loss with adversarial training (relativistic GAN loss with R3GAN backbone) to mitigate artifacts and improve detail fidelity in low-NFE regimes, with a clear ablation showing consistent FID gains (Table 2, Table 4, Figure 4) and evidence that this does not induce mode collapse (Table 8, precision/recall/density/coverage metrics).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 6 datasets (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2, LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256, MS-COCO/Stable Diffusion) and consistent improvements over strong baselines (UniPC, iPNDM, LD3, S4S) across most NFE settings.

Thorough and thoughtful ablation studies addressing many natural reviewer concerns preemptively: theoretical guidance ablation, GAN loss type, adversarial loss weight sensitivity, mode collapse, dataset-size efficiency, cross-dataset generalization (Table 7), training time/memory/inference-time overhead, and comparison with consistency distillation for diversity preservation.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1), extensive hyperparameter and setup documentation in the appendix, and use of publicly available datasets/checkpoints.
Qualitative samples (Figs 8-25) support the quantitative claims, showing visually closer match to teacher outputs than baseline solvers at matched NFE.
weaknesses: Performance at very low NFE (1-2) is explicitly weaker than the simple DPM-Solver baseline (Appendix B.8, Table 11), which is a notable limitation since ultra-low-NFE acceleration is often the primary motivating use case for such training-based solvers.

Training cost is non-trivial and larger than the lightweight baselines it targets to improve upon: GAS requires 2-9 hours vs <1 hour for LD3/S4S, partially undercutting the framing of the approach as a lightweight alternative to full distillation.

The method still requires backpropagation through the full multi-step solver trajectory, which the authors acknowledge limits scalability to larger resolutions/models, and separate training is needed per target NFE, reducing practical flexibility.

The core technical contribution is largely a recombination of known ideas (theoretically-guided additive coefficient corrections generalizing LD3/S4S, plus adversarial distillation losses already used in diffusion distillation literature such as Sauer et al. and Kim et al.), making the novelty more incremental/engineering-oriented than conceptually groundbreaking.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting for FID scores across the many tables, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of some of the smaller reported gaps (e.g., MS-COCO NFE=7 where GAS is slightly worse than Best LD3: 11.36 vs 10.83).

The adversarial component depends on a separately pretrained/initialized discriminator (R3GAN architecture) whose sensitivity to architecture choice or transfer across substantially different domains is not deeply explored beyond loss-weight ablation.

Improvements over strong training-free solvers diminish at higher NFE (e.g., CIFAR10 NFE=10: GAS 2.17 vs teacher 2.03), suggesting the practical benefit window is concentrated in a specific low-to-moderate NFE regime.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant problem (fast diffusion ODE solving via trainable solver/timestep parameterization) and proposes a reasonably well-motivated generalization of prior solver-distillation parameterizations (LD3, S4S) that unifies them under a single signature (Table 1), with additive theoretical guidance from a base multistep solver (DPM-Solver++(3M)).

Extensive empirical evaluation across six datasets/settings spanning pixel space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2) and latent space (LSUN-Bedroom, class-conditional ImageNet, MS-COCO with Stable Diffusion), covering a wide range of NFE budgets.

Thorough ablation studies in the appendix: contribution of theoretical guidance (B.1), choice of adversarial loss (B.2), training dynamics/convergence stability (B.3), cross-dataset generalization (B.4), adversarial loss weight sensitivity (B.5), mode-collapse/diversity checks via precision/recall/density/coverage (B.6), comparison with consistency distillation (B.7), alternative coefficient parameterizations (B.9), and resource analysis (dataset size, training time, memory, inference time, Appendix C).

Reasonably detailed reproducibility information: full algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 1), hyperparameters, optimizer settings, and teacher-generation protocols are given for every experimental setting (Appendix D).

The qualitative samples (Figs. 8-25) are provided across many NFE/dataset combinations and visually support the claim that GAS narrows the gap to the teacher model, including removing artifacts relative to GS/UniPC at low NFE.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: the Generalized Solver is mainly a more flexible re-parameterization of existing LD3/S4S-style solver distillation (effectively adding a weighted sum of past points and additive rather than purely multiplicative theoretical corrections), and combining a regression/distillation loss with an adversarial loss on top of a frozen teacher is a well-established recipe in diffusion distillation (e.g., ADD, LADD, consistency-trajectory methods, Kim et al. 2023), so the main contribution is largely an engineering combination of known ideas rather than a fundamentally new concept.

Reported gains over the strongest baselines are inconsistent and often marginal at higher NFE: e.g., on CIFAR10 the advantage over S4S-Alt nearly vanishes by NFE=8-10 (2.25 vs 2.25, 2.17 vs 2.18); on AFHQv2, GAS is actually worse than S4S-Alt at NFE=8 and NFE=10 (2.31 vs 2.29 and 2.31 vs 2.18); on LSUN-Bedroom at NFE=4 GAS (6.68) underperforms the training-free UniPC[DMN] baseline (4.55); on ImageNet at NFE=7 GAS (4.32) is worse than Best-LD3 (4.16). This undermines the claim of uniformly 'superior performance' stated in the abstract/discussion.

The method requires separate training per target NFE and per dataset (acknowledged as a limitation), and training cost for GAS is substantial relative to training-free solvers—up to several hours with GPU-heavy discriminator training (R3GAN) and up to tens of GB peak memory—reducing the practical appeal of the 'lightweight' framing emphasized in the introduction.

Performance at very low NFE (1-2), arguably the most practically interesting/competitive regime versus one-step distillation methods, is explicitly reported as poor (Appendix B.8), limiting the significance of the contribution exactly where acceleration research is most needed.
The abstract states 'Code is available at' with no actual link provided, raising reproducibility and completeness concerns despite the otherwise detailed appendix.

Some ablations (e.g., Table 3 fair comparison with S4S, Table 10 comparison with LMS/LMS+PC) are run under the paper's own codebase/hyperparameters rather than the official baseline implementations, which could bias comparisons in the proposed method's favor; similarly, Table 2 notes that some baseline FIDs are taken directly from other papers with potentially different teacher hyperparameters, flagged by a dagger, which weakens the apples-to-apples nature of the main comparison table.

No theoretical analysis (e.g., convergence guarantees, approximation error bounds) is provided for the proposed additive-guidance parameterization beyond the empirical ablation; the claimed inductive-bias benefit is only supported indirectly via FID numbers.

The adversarial training component adds a non-trivial number of additional design choices and hyperparameters (relativistic loss, gradient penalty coefficients, discriminator architecture/training schedule) that somewhat contradicts the paper's stated goal of avoiding 'intricate training techniques,' and increases the complexity/instability risk typical of GAN-based training even if mode collapse is checked for one setting (ImageNet, NFE=4).

strengths: Introduces a clean generalization of linear multi-step solver parameterization (Generalized Solver) that embeds theoretical coefficients (e.g., from DPM-Solver++(3M)) as additive guidance rather than learning multiplicative corrections from scratch, addressing documented instabilities in prior work (LD3, S4S) such as unstable loss scale and limited parameter disentanglement.

Combines the distillation objective with adversarial training (relativistic GAN loss + gradient penalty, based on R3GAN) to specifically target fine-grained detail/artifact removal in low-NFE regimes, and shows this is complementary to the solver parameterization.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six datasets spanning pixel-space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2) and latent-space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256, Stable Diffusion on MS-COCO) models, with consistent improvements over strong baselines (UniPC, iPNDM, LD3, S4S/S4S-Alt) across multiple NFE settings.

Very thorough ablation studies in the appendix: theoretical guidance ablation, GAN loss type (traditional vs relativistic), FID progression during training, generalization across datasets, adversarial loss weight sensitivity, mode collapse/diversity checks (precision/recall/density/coverage), training dataset size reduction, training time, and memory usage.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: explicit algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detailed hyperparameters for every experimental setting, and use of publicly available datasets/checkpoints.
The paper candidly reports failure modes/limitations, e.g., poor performance at NFE=1,2 and increased training time/compute with adversarial loss, rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the Generalized Solver is largely an additive-correction extension of existing LD3/S4S parameterizations, and adversarial training augmentation of distillation losses is a well-established technique in diffusion distillation (e.g., Sauer et al., Kim et al., Yin et al.) applied here to solver distillation specifically; the core contribution is more of a careful engineering combination than a fundamentally new idea.

The method still requires separate training for each desired inference NFE, and incorporating the adversarial loss increases training time substantially (roughly 2-9x versus GS alone, per Appendix C.2/Table 13-14), which somewhat undercuts the paper's stated motivation of being a lightweight, resource-constrained alternative to full distillation, especially for large-scale models like video diffusion mentioned in the introduction.

Performance at very low NFE (1-2) remains weak (Appendix B.8), which is precisely the regime where acceleration methods are most valuable; this limits the practical significance of the contribution in the most demanding use cases.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on FID (and LPIPS as the training/ablation loss); no human evaluation or complementary quality/text-alignment metrics (e.g., CLIP score for the Stable Diffusion experiments) are reported, which is a concern given adversarial losses can improve FID/perceptual similarity without necessarily improving all aspects of sample fidelity or diversity.

Baseline comparisons for the text-to-image Stable Diffusion setting are narrower (only LD3/GITS/iPNDM variants) compared to the richer baseline set used for pixel/latent experiments; no comparison with other recent fast adversarial distillation methods (e.g., ADD/SDXL-Turbo-style approaches) that target the same regime, even if just for context.

The generalization claims across datasets (Appendix B.4) are only tested between closely related domains (FFHQ and AFHQv2, both 64x64 faces/animals), so the broader claim of cross-dataset applicability is not strongly substantiated.
